blocks.text: Cap how many requests are admitted per unit of time, rejecting or delaying the excess.

A rate limiter protects a service from callers, whether buggy, abusive or just popular. The **token bucket** is the common algorithm: tokens refill at a steady rate up to a capacity, and each request spends one. The capacity allows short **bursts**; the refill rate sets the long-run average.

items: **Token bucket:** bursts up to capacity, steady average rate.
**Fixed or sliding window:** count requests per interval; simpler, with boundary spikes in the fixed form.
**Leaky bucket:** smooths output to a constant rate.

blocks.text: A rejection should say when to come back. HTTP 429 with `Retry-After` turns a limit into a protocol the client can follow.

walkthrough.note: Tokens refill lazily from elapsed time on each call, so no timer thread exists. Time comes from an injected supplier, which makes the behavior testable.
One bucket per client key, created on first use, so one noisy client cannot spend another's allowance. A real map needs eviction.
Capacity 3, refill 2 per second. Client `a` bursts three, is refused with a wait, gets one after 500 ms, and is full again after ten seconds, capped at three.

blocks.text: A public API with per-key quotas.

A SaaS API gives each key 100 requests per second with bursts of 200. A customer's retry loop goes wrong and floods the API. The limiter sits at the gateway, keyed by API key, and answers 429 with a `Retry-After` header. Well-behaved clients back off, the runaway customer only hurts itself, and other tenants are unaffected. Limits across several gateway nodes need shared state, usually in Redis.
Payoff: abuse and accidents are contained per client, and compliant clients get a clear signal for when to retry.

lists.title: Use when
items: You expose an API and must contain abusive or buggy clients.
A downstream has a known throughput ceiling or a paid quota.
Fairness among tenants matters more than peak throughput.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The real limit is concurrency, not arrival rate: use a [Bulkhead](kata:bulkhead).
Rejecting requests is worse than queueing them for a short time.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Fixed windows allow double the rate across a window boundary.
Per-node limiters multiply the limit by the node count.
Unbounded per-key maps are a memory leak under key churn.
Skewed clocks: use a monotonic source such as `System.nanoTime`.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: The JDK has no rate limiter; use Bucket4j, Resilience4j or Guava's `RateLimiter` rather than hand-rolling for production.
Per-key state is a `ConcurrentHashMap` problem; evict idle keys or use a cache with expiry.

rows.difference: A rate limiter caps arrivals per second; a bulkhead caps concurrent work in progress. A slow dependency can overload you at a low rate, which only a bulkhead catches.
The limiter says no; backoff with jitter is how a good client responds, ideally honoring `Retry-After`.
A limiter protects the callee by shaping incoming load. A breaker protects the caller by reacting to the callee's failures.
Gateways are the usual place to enforce per-client limits before requests reach services.
Timeouts bound how long a request may take once started; rate limits bound how many may start.

options.why: A budget refills with elapsed time up to a burst cap, and each admitted request spends one unit.
Nothing is released when work finishes; the budget depends on time, not on work in progress.
Admission does not depend on failures of a downstream, only on the earned budget.
No call is being bounded in duration; the method only decides whether a request may start.

exercises.scenario: Your public API has a customer whose script sometimes sends 5,000 requests in a second, degrading latency for everyone. Normal clients send a handful per second. You want to contain the heavy client and tell it when to retry.

options.why: A per-key token bucket contains the heavy client and can return 429 with a retry hint.
It caps concurrency, but a fast stream of cheap requests can still overload you at low concurrency.
No downstream is failing; the load is the problem, and it comes from one caller.
That is the client's side of the story; it does nothing to protect the server.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line that lets idle clients take unlimited bursts.
exercises.explanation: Tokens accumulate without bound while a client is idle, so after an hour it can burst thousands of requests. Clamp the refill: `tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + earned)`.

exercises.prompt: Order the token bucket's acquire step.
exercises.explanation: Read the clock, refill from the elapsed time, record the new timestamp, reject if less than one token remains, and only then spend a token.

exercises.prompt: Explain how a token bucket works and what burst capacity and refill rate each control.

modelAnswer.text: A bucket holds up to a capacity of tokens and refills at a fixed rate, computed lazily from elapsed time. Each request spends a token; with none left it is rejected, ideally with a retry hint. Capacity sets how large a burst is allowed; the refill rate sets the sustained average.

keyPoints: Tokens refill at a steady rate, capped at capacity
Each request spends a token; none left means reject
Capacity controls burst size, refill rate the average
Lazy refill from elapsed time and an injected clock
Reject with a retry hint; keep one bucket per client
